062rh0sg2r.description:
Healthcare is where open source stops being ideology and starts becoming accountability. A bug is not just a bug. A failed deployment is not just downtime. The software has to work for doctors, nurses, patients, community workers, hospitals, NGOs, and governments, in difficult real-world conditions.

This talk is the story of Open Healthcare Network and CARE, how a FOSS project that started during a public health crisis grew into an open healthcare Digital Public Good used across real deployments.

I will share what it takes to move from a GitHub repository to public health infrastructure; building clinical workflows, designing reusable healthcare primitives, managing implementation feedback, supporting government and NGO deployments, and keeping the project open while protecting reliability and trust.

The talk will go behind the visible product and focus on the systems that actually make high-stakes FOSS survive, contributor onboarding, review culture, documentation, release discipline, governance, security expectations, and community ownership.

CARE’s journey has involved 1300+ contributors across the ecosystem, real hospital and community health workflows, TeleICU deployments, palliative care grids, and public-good infrastructure that must be self-hostable, adaptable, and free from vendor lock-in.Lastly, on how have setup Open Healthcare Network Foundation as a long-term steward for healthcare FOSS and its real world challenges.

The talk will be a field report from building FOSS in one of the hardest domains. I will share what worked, what broke, what we had to relearn, and what other FOSS projects can borrow when they want to become durable public infrastructure.
keyTakeaways: How a FOSS project can grow from crisis response into long-term public infrastructure.
Why community is not a side activity, but core infrastructure for a serious open-source project.
What changes when open-source software is used in healthcare, government programs, and real field operations.
How CARE balances technical architecture, clinical workflows, standards, deployment realities, and contributor energy.
How to build trust around FOSS: through documentation, governance, release discipline, security, and implementation feedback loops.
Lessons for maintainers who want their projects to move beyond GitHub adoption into real-world social impact.

2bfslonj72.description:
The Centre for Open-source Software and Hardware (COSH) at NITK Surathkal was established with a simple but important goal: to answer the question that many students, faculty members, and organizations struggle with: "How do I get started with open source?". This talk will share the journey of building COSH as one of India's first dedicated academic centers focused on open-source software and hardware, and how it evolved from an institutional initiative into a thriving community of contributors, maintainers, researchers, and industry collaborators.

The talk will discuss the strategies, challenges, and lessons learned while fostering a hacker and open-source culture within an Indian academic institution. It will cover how COSH helps newcomers take their first steps in open source, guides them through making meaningful contributions, and supports participation in flagship programs such as Google Summer of Code (GSoC) and Linux Foundation mentorship initiatives. Several students have grown into maintainers of open-source projects and modules, as well as mentors and organization administrators in programs such as GSoC.

The resulting ecosystem has enabled students and faculty to contribute to projects with real-world impact, including the migration of NITK's campus network of more than 40,000 devices to IPv6, the development of a network emulation platform adopted by multiple industries, contributions to packet scheduling algorithms that are now part of the Linux networking stack, and the development of the quantum networking module in ns-3. Notably, nearly half of these open-source initiatives have been supported by industry and research funding.
keyTakeaways: How to build a structured pathway for students to move from first-time contributors to open-source maintainers within an academic institution?
Practical strategies for creating and sustaining a FOSS culture in a formal university setting, balancing curriculum, research, and community-driven work.
Lessons from establishing COSH as a bridge between academia, industry, and global open-source ecosystems.
How open-source projects can be integrated into institutional work, leading to outcomes such as IPv6 campus migration, Linux kernel contributions, and research-grade systems?
The role of mentorship pipelines and external programs (GSoC, LFX, etc.) in accelerating student growth into global open-source contributors.
Insights into how industry-funded open-source development can align academic research with production-level impact and sustainability.
Approaches for building a self-sustaining ecosystem where students evolve into mentors, maintainers, and community leaders over time.

8s4g5qj3oq.description:
One of the biggest obstacles a beginner faces with a programming language, especially one outside the mainstream, is the install: toolchains, package managers, editor setup, and version skew that derail a learner before they write a line of code.

This talk is about a course book that removes that barrier. For NPTEL's "Functional Programming with OCaml" MOOC (twelve modules, taught to students across India), the book is a fully client-side, zero-install website: every example runs in the reader's browser, with nothing installed and no server behind it. It scales from a first "hello, world" to OxCaml (a cutting-edge OCaml extension for performance and safety) and a full Linux VM, dev tools and all, that boots in the browser tab to explore memory-safety issues and build unikernels.

The book reads like a notebook, and a single markdown source produces all three views: the page, a reveal.js slide deck, and the runnable cells, so the slides cannot drift from the prose. Quizzes are built into the same format: multiple-choice with explanations, and code-completion challenges whose hidden tests run in the browser. Following the Brown PLT group's quiz study of the Rust Book (Crichton and Krishnamurthi, OOPSLA 2024), the quizzes record anonymous responses that show where readers get stuck, enabling targeted edits to be measured.

Under the hood, it is FOSS end-to-end: the OCaml toolchain compiled to JavaScript with js_of_ocaml, the x-ocaml WebComponent for the cells, and a client-side Linux VM. I will share some engineering lessons, including shrinking the OxCaml bundle from 285 MB to 4 MB so it could be hosted at all (GitHub rejects files over 100 MB), and the trade-offs of running a toolchain in a browser sandbox.

The book was drafted from existing lecture material with heavy LLM assistance under careful pedagogical review, and I will give an honest account of where AI helped and where it failed. What keeps it trustworthy: every code snippet is machine-checked by mdx, OCaml's documentation-testing tool, which compiles each example and verifies its output, so a broken or hallucinated snippet fails the build instead of reaching a student.

None of this is specific to OCaml. Any educator can build interactive, zero-install material on a FOSS stack, and the entire book and its toolchain are open.
keyTakeaways: Why "zero install, runs in the browser" is the right default for teaching programming, and the accessibility case for students on constrained machines and networks.
The FOSS stack that makes it work: js_of_ocaml, the x-ocaml WebComponent, and a client-side Linux VM, with no server.
Engineering lessons from shipping a full language toolchain as a static site, including a 285 MB to 4 MB bundle diet to clear GitHub's 100 MB file limit.
One markdown source for the page, the slides, and interactive quizzes, plus a quiz-analytics loop (after the Brown study of the Rust Book) that targets improvements.
LLM-assisted authoring under human review, with every code snippet machine-checked by mdx: what worked, what did not.

The year was 2020. Like many Linux users, I was deep into distro hopping, tweaking my setup, and slowly shaping my desktop into something that felt truly mine. One small part of that setup was a GNOME extension called Simple Net Speed, which showed my internet speed in the top bar. It worked (mostly). But there was one tiny thing that kept annoying me. The extension updated the speed in UI every 3 seconds. That meant it could show 500 kbps for a while and then suddenly jump to 5 MBps. It was a small issue, but once I noticed it, I could not unsee it. I was completely new to open source at the time, but I did what any frustrated developer eventually does: I opened the code and tried to fix it.

That became my first-ever pull request: change the update interval from 3 seconds to 1 second. A small fix. A tiny change. But for me, it was the beginning. The maintainer didn’t looked over my PR.

So I closed the PR, created a branch called simple-net-speed-simplified, and went all in. In four days, I made 108 commits. Eventually, I realized that the original extension solved the maintainer’s problem, but not necessarily the community’s. So I renamed my version and released it as Net Speed Simplified.

What started as a one-line frustration slowly turned into a full fork. I added more customization, rewrote major parts of the extension, improved the install flow, and kept polishing it based on what users actually wanted. My pull request back to the original project is still open today, with 354 commits. But now, the fork has become its own project.

This journey also became my crash course in open source. One contributor, Mohith from IIT Varanasi, helped rewrite large parts of the codebase into modern JavaScript. That is one of my favorite parts of open source: people from different backgrounds, ages, and experience levels coming together to improve something small but genuinely useful.

Today, both projects continue to exist. The original has around 80 stars and 270K+ downloads. My fork, Net Speed Simplified, has around 130 stars and 208K+ downloads. It may be one of those rare cases where a fork ended up with more stars and almost as many downloads as the original.

In this talk, I will share the story of how a tiny fix born out of frustration became my first GitHub repository, taught me open source, introduced me to community collaboration, and eventually reached more than 200K users.

Target AudienceThis talk is for anyone who is curious about getting started with open source, especially beginners, first-time contributors, Linux and GNOME users, and developers who have ever noticed a bug or missing feature in a tool they use but have not yet taken the effort to fix it themselves.

ConclusionAttendees will leave with one simple idea: you do not need permission, experience, or a grand plan to begin contributing to open source. Sometimes, all it takes is one small frustration, one tiny fix, and the willingness to keep going. That small step can teach you new skills, connect you with people, and open doors you never expected.
keyTakeaways: If you face a problem, think you can fix it, and the thing is open source, then go for it.
You don’t need permission to keep going, if you feel like contributions aren’t working out, just fork it and maintain it.
Keep iterating on the thing you built and listen to community feedback.
Open-Source project teaches more than any JavaScript or Git crash course would teach you.
Open source connects you with people of all ages and experience around.
Forking isn’t a fight. A fork and original can co-exist with different set of users in focus.

Over the last ten years, working with Indian public data has come a long way. Problems of access are becoming a thing of the past, while the need for context has become greater than ever. After moving out of Indian newsrooms, I have with my team been working on building out Data For India, a public platform to advance the understanding of India, through data.

In this talk, I will first explain a little bit about our process behind asking questions, doing research and collating the data, as well as the communication including visualisation, with examples. I will then focus on the role of open data in our process and our work; this will include our thinking about the data we choose to use, the format we currently share it in, and our aim to play a larger role in the open data community. Lastly, I will share some key learnings about the state of Indian public data, and some thoughts, hopes and concerns about the way ahead. With the advancement of integrated tools to access Indian public data, including MCP servers, there is a great opportunity to further democratise access to data. Using some examples, I will talk about some of the transformative things that we have learned about the country through access to unit-level data. However, through a few examples, I will also highlight the challenges this brings with it, and the dangers of losing context.

Two themes will run through the talk:

One: moving away from false binaries, including those between tech/ data and social sciences research/ communication.

Two: pushing ourselves to expand our vision of what happens next.

If the ultimate aim of open data is for knowledge to advance and decision-making to get better - whether for governments, private companies or individuals - I will end the talk with some thoughts on what's needed to close this gap, technically, conceptually, pedagogically and democratically.

cpno9khavs.description:
Neer Vazhvu (neervazhvu.org) is an open-source platform that turns scattered public water data into living, interactive maps. It is live across three Indian cities (Chennai, Madurai and Bengaluru), with a fourth, Mumbai, in progress, built by a very small team.

The starting problem: a city's water data sits in many separate silos, across different departments, portals, and formats, so no one sees the whole picture and the warning signs get missed.

The heart of the talk is architecture: how we serve several cities from one codebase. A new city is mostly configuration, data, and capability flags rather than a forked codebase, and I will be honest about where that discipline holds and where it leaks.

How the system is designed for partners to contribute data without us as the bottleneck: fixed layer contracts plus ingest and validation scripts, so onboarding a new river basin is meant to be a manifest and a data drop rather than a rewrite.

The data pipelines: parsing government PDFs, portals, and satellite imagery into standardized, provenance-tagged layers.

The honest part: the code is the easy bit. Curated, maintained, trustworthy data is the hard one. I will cover what "open" really means here, why open source and open data are different problems, and the open question of how a civic project stays both open and sustainable.

A live demo across the cities.
keyTakeaways: A reusable pattern for building multi-city civic platforms from one codebase, using configuration and capability flags instead of forking.
A clear-eyed distinction between open source and open data, and what each means for a public-interest project.
A realistic picture of what it takes to sustain open civic infrastructure with a very small team and almost no budget.

advandigma.description:
Zasper started out as an open-source project focused on expanding and improving the capabilities of Project Jupyter. This talk reports on how the project has evolved in terms of adoption.

Many FOSS talks focus on how to get your first 10,000 users. This talk is about what happens when you build something highly specialized and discover your user graph isn't wide—it’s deep. Zasper (a high-performance, Go-backed Jupyter IDE) secured a FOSS United grant and initially saw high broad adoption post-launch. However, as the initial curiosity tapered off and those general numbers went down, a unique reality emerged: low broad adoption, but extreme usage intensity from a core cohort of power users. I'll share the architectural decisions that kept those power users hooked, the realities of balancing independent contracting with open-source stewardship, and why retention is the ultimate validator for a niche developer tool.
keyTakeaways: The core thesis: Why standard Jupyter setups struggle under heavy logs, massive datasets, and complex rendering.
Choosing Go for an interactive notebook IDE backend—leveraging its low-overhead concurrency and runtime efficiency to fix the performance gap.
Securing the FOSS United grant: Moving from a personal side project to a community-backed initiative.
Launching: Taking a step back to focus on what’s actually needed
Deconstructing the post-launch metrics: Facing the reality of high to low raw download counts.
Discovering the "Deep Graph": Spotting the intense, multi-hour daily usage patterns of a dedicated cohort.
Deep Dive: The precise engineering choices (state synchronization, low-latency communication via goroutines) that made the tool indispensable to these power users.
The balancing act: Managing the demands of open-source stewardship
Shifting community strategy: Why prioritizing deep feature stability for 14,000 power users matters more than building a funnel for 50,000 casual clickers.
A lightning-fast live demo showcasing Zasper running smoothly under heavy stress loads.
Final takeaway: Why retention, not virality, is the true indicator of product-market fit in developer tooling.

0k2f61lkrj.description:
India holds one of the world's most diverse repositories of knowledge — millions of manuscripts, rare printed texts, regional-language books residing in private collections, temple libraries, and local archives. However, the vast majority of it this material exists only in physical form or uncatalogued, and quietly decaying. Most Indian custodians of rare texts lack the budget, technical capacity, or access to commercial digitization services. Traditional Institutional archiving efforts, where they exist, are slow, expensive, and often inaccessible to the communities whose heritage is at stake. The result is an asymmetric loss: the texts and knowledge systems most underrepresented in global digital archives are precisely those most at risk of permanent disappearance.

At ServantsOfKnowledge, we asked: what if any community — a small library, a local trust, a university archive — could build and operate its own digitization pipeline using open hardware and open software?

We have been building open infrastructure to change this. While our open-source book scanner hardware designs are already publicly available, at IndiaFOSS 2026, we are completing the pipeline with the public release of Repub.

Repub workflow - an end-to-end, fully open-source stack that takes a physical book from shelf to searchable, publishable digital artifact.

Repub is a software piece that lives alongside our scanners. The moment a digitization session ends, Repub takes over the scanner's output and runs it through a post-processing pipeline:

Cropping: Using image processing libraries to extract the page boundaries of a book

Deskewing: Rotate the pages in case they are slanted

Dewarping: Removing warping that happens during scanning of a thick book

Searchable PDFs — with embedded OCR text layers

Structured metadata — enabling cataloguing and discovery

Multiple end-user formats — so the output is immediately usable, not just stored

This talk covers:

The crisis of unarchived knowledge in India and why open tools are the only scalable answer

How Repub works: challenges and the solutions

How it integrates with our open hardware scanners to form a complete pipeline

Already in production with 100K books being procesed

The public release: how to get it, use it, and contribute

What's next: a future open-source library management system designed for Indian research institutions

The pipeline is designed to run on commodity hardware, requires No prior archiving or software experience and is fully automated. It handles the hardest part of digitization: turning raw scans into documents that can actually be read, searched, and used by researchers, students, and the public. If you have a belief that India's knowledge belongs to everyone, a quick Digitization Schooling at ServantsOfKnowledge Academy to get you started.

Repub is one piece of a longer roadmap. ServantsOfKnowledge is also developing a next-generation library management system designed specifically for Indian research institutions — built to handle the scale, script diversity, and metadata complexity of India's collections. This too will be open-sourced.

This is FOSS applied to cultural infrastructure. This project demonstrates that FOSS is not only for software products, it is a governance model for cultural infrastructure. Every component we release i.e. hardware, software, documentation lowers the barrier for any community in India to begin archiving their own heritage. The tools do not require institutional budgets or vendor lock-in. They require only the will to preserve.
keyTakeaways: A concrete mental model of how open hardware + open software can address a real, urgent social problem
A vision for what community-owned archiving infrastructure can look like at scale in India
Practical starting points if they want to adopt or contribute to the workflow
A clear on-ramp for contributing to the project
A deeper appreciation for what "digital commons" means in an Indian context

42vnv417j4.description:
Most developer communities fail the same way: they start with a burst of enthusiasm, attract a core of deeply committed people, and then plateau. The outer ring never grows because the barrier to entry is too high. Or the opposite — the community stays wide and shallow, lots of followers, no one doing real work.

A model that works is concentric layers, each requiring progressively more commitment. The outer layers handle distribution and bring in casual interest. The inner ones build the committed core that sustains everything else. You need both, and you need to build them in roughly the right order.

This talk draws on direct experience building LLVM Social Bangalore (600 → 3,500 members, the world's largest compiler meetup), IICT (India's premier compilers workshop, now in its third year at IISc), SEGFAULT (India's first compiler hackathon), and Point Blank (a student tech community that has produced 20+ FOSS contributors and multiple Hackathon winning teams).

Layer 1 — Distribution. Pick a platform where your target audience already lives, not where you wish they were. Add a Discourse forum as institutional memory and a YouTube channel for recorded talks. Content compounds; chat archives don't.

Layer 2 — Open Source Programs. GSoC, LFX, and their India-local equivalents (KWOC, DWOC, SLOP) are underused community-building tools. They're not just about getting code written — they create contributors who feel ownership, and they function as a direct pipeline into deeper involvement. The operational prerequisite is a well-structured GitHub org with good-first-issue labels and a getting-started guide. Without that, motivated contributors bounce.

Layer 3 — Hackathons. Not all formats are equal. 24-hour onsite events produce shallow work in technically deep domains. Month-long online events have terrible completion rates. Hybrid hackathons — online rounds with mentored check-ins, in-person finals — consistently outperform both. SEGFAULT uses this model. Smart India Hackathon uses it. It works.

Layer 4 — Meetups and Tech Talks. Regular meetups are the connective tissue of a community. Mix invited talks with paper-reading sessions, low-agenda coffee meetups, and structured beginner workshops — they serve different audiences. LLVM Social Bangalore's Introduction to Common Compiler Tools series (10 talks, 800+ attendees online) brought more people into the community than any single conference.

Layer 5 — Schools and cohorts. A summer or winter school with real admission standards — and internship offers for top performers — reaches students who would never find their way to a research lab otherwise. No certificates keeps the cohort motivated.

Layer 6 — Conferences and Devrooms. IndiaFOSS devrooms are the most accessible entry point: FOSS United handles the logistics, organizers curate the room. A devroom is the proving ground before a standalone conference becomes viable.

Layer 7 — 1:1 Mentoring. The highest-leverage intervention for individuals. A student with a year of sustained mentorship from someone who's already done the thing they're trying to do ends up in a fundamentally different position than one who only attends talks.

The pieces don't have to happen in strict order — but they compound. Each layer makes the others easier to sustain.
keyTakeaways: A concrete, layered framework you can apply to any technical community — from a college club to a national conference series
How to pick the right platform for your audience, and why getting this wrong early costs you months
Why open source programs (GSoC, LFX, and their Indian equivalents) are one of the highest-leverage community-building tools most organisers never use deliberately
Which hackathon format actually works for technical domains, and which ones waste everyone's time
How to structure a meetup series so it serves beginners, practitioners, and researchers simultaneously — rather than optimising for just one group
When a devroom is the right move and when to attempt a standalone conference
How the layers compound: practical sequencing advice so you're not trying to run a conference before you have a community

9ojc3pnp7u.description:
The <div> on the left is identical to the <div> on the right and yet the one on the left renders 1.5x faster than the one on the right. This happens because each pixel of the <div> on right requires the context of the pixel under it as it is not completely opaque, on the other hand the <div> on the right doesn’t even need to render the pixels under it. Having many them can unknowingly butcher the performance of your UI.

We at Mecha are building a GUI Library for the Mecha Comet, and we have found that there is a lot hidden under hoods of GUI Libraries that let’s them render any kind of UI efficiently. I am going to go over a few algorithms and concepts like early-z discard, painter’s algorithm, alpha blending and damaged rendering that are implemented in GUI Libraries like Flutter and even in the engine behind Chromium to improve the performance of UIs. We will also go over how they integrate with each other — how a single design choice (like whether a surface is opaque or translucent) decides which of these optimizations the renderer can use. Without these algorithms it would be prohibitively expensive to render the kinds of UI we see everywhere at a reasonable resource usage.

Now that the listeners have an understanding of the above concepts, I’ll go over how they can use these concepts to improve performance of UIs in the design phase and/or the development phase. I’ll go over elements that just improve the performance without any drawbacks, and also talk about the hidden costs of using certain element so listeners can consciously pick them rather than unknowingly paying the price.

658mrgdc1b.description:
FQ-PIE is a Networking Active Queue Management algorithm, developed by a research team at NITK, Surathkal. It's main utility is to reduce latency and improve throughput for Internet traffic, which ends up passing through several, long buffers. There is an active effort to get this algorithm standardized and adopted by the community.

I got interested in trying to improve the support for FQ-PIE, as well as incorporate feedback from various interested communities. Having previously only been a consumer of FOSS, ended up going down a deep rabbit hole of contributing to FOSS! Since an Open Standard can be looked at as a specification, supporting its implementation can differ depending on the different consumers, layer of software abstraction, environments, etc. This provided a unique opportunity to:

Discover different FOSS networking projects, and how the processes and contributing style can differ vastly between them.

Collaborating with maintainers & community members, receiving criticizm and feedback, and looping this back into the Standards themselves.

This talk covers all of these, and also welcomes contributors to FQ-PIE, and FOSS in general.
keyTakeaways: What is FQ-PIE, and what are Open Standards
How I was able to contribute to making FQ-PIE better by contributing to FOSS
The networking FOSS projects involved, the unique experience contributing to each of them, and learnings overall.
How anyone can contribute to FOSS, and how it becomes even easier to do so when it contributes to a clearer overall goal, like improving Open Standards.

bemvjh2dac.description:
India’s public data is extensive but exists in silos, and often in non-machine-readable formats. Census tables, NFHS health surveys, electoral rolls, and poverty estimates are all often published as PDF reports. As a data enthusiast or a policy maker, turning these reports into actionable insights for India becomes a classic last-mile delivery problem – how to make sense of this data?

BharatViz (https://bharatviz.org/, http://github.com/saketlab/bharatviz) fixes the last-mile problem by providing a dashboard for getting a publication-quality choropleth given a CSV of state/district/regions. It supports various input formats, including CSV and spreadsheets, and produces a visualisation in under five seconds.

Under the hood, Bharatviz is a static React + D3 app that renders every choropleth client-side as SVG, a thin Express/TypeScript API for PNG/PDF export and the MCP layer, and a geospatial corpus served as flat GeoJSON and GeoParquet via a CDN. Bharatviz hosts geojsons for more than 3,000 cities, as well as admin and subadmin boundaries from different rounds of the census (1872-2011), including the latest district boundaries, with a crosswalk dictionary. BharatViz comes with R and Python development kits for easy integration with Jupyter and R notebooks. BharatViz allows you to generate choropleths with just a call to its API. The MCP server provides an interface for coding agents to make sense of the Indian boundaries, and demography to enable queries like “How many hospitals are there in my pin code 400071” or "Which 20 districts have the lowest literacy rates — and what do they have in common?" or "Does the Meta wealth index predict literacy across districts? And are tribal districts poorer?".

In this lightning talk, I will introduce BharatViz, outline its core architecture, and walk through some case studies using the API. One such use case is the district-level pollution tracker. I will also demonstrate the MCP and some use cases around it.
keyTakeaways: BharatViz makes mapping extremely quick and easy
BharatViz API enables mapping scriptable, generating maps without ever leaving your IDE
BharatViz MCP enables lets coding agents to answer real analytical questions on India and its admin/subadmin boundaries and facilities/demographics

dticdhpupe.description:
For someone running a small business, money discipline is supposed to come "later, when things stabilise." The trouble is that things never stabilise.

A friend of mine runs a gym in Chennai. About a year ago he showed me his Excel sheet and admitted he had no idea if he was profitable. Tax time was a panic every year. He paid himself last, and often paid himself nothing. He had looked at Mindbody and Glofox, but they were priced for the US. The Indian alternatives he tried felt closed, and he did not trust them with his money data. So he was back on Excel.

That conversation stuck with me. India has roughly 50,000 small, owner-run gyms with the same problem, and the software market for them is either too expensive, proprietary with lock-in, or a spreadsheet. For a category that handles people's money, having nothing open or self-hostable felt off.

NetGainz is what I have built since then. It is a finance and operations platform for microgyms, released under AGPLv3, built on Frappe and ERPNext with a Next.js frontend. The product is opinionated around Profit First, Mike Michalowicz's small-business cash-flow method that flips the standard formula into Sales minus Profit equals Expenses.

In this talk I want to share what I have actually learned in a year, the parts I got wrong included. I started with the MIT license and switched to AGPLv3 a few months in, and there is a story there worth telling. I went with site-per-tenant over a shared database because for finance data the isolation matters more than the operational cost. I built the frontend as a separate Next.js app rather than staying with Frappe's Vue stack, and that had real tradeoffs both ways. The most surprising thing has been how quickly the technical decisions started shaping the business model, and the business decisions started shaping the code.

The wider point I want to make is that the same approach works for many other underserved Indian SMB verticals: yoga studios, music schools, tuition centres, small clinics, NGOs. I am calling the pattern FOSS for the Forgotten Middle. In the talk I will share how to pick a vertical and how to set up a project to invite contribution from day one.

The other reason I want to give this talk is to invite the IndiaFOSS community to contribute. If you have ever looked at a small-business problem in India and thought "someone should open-source this," this talk is for you. I will have good-first-issues labelled before the conference and the repo is at github.com/lokashche/netgainz.

ck74mbe1ds.description:
In 2025, IndiaFOSS was the first in-person developer event I ever attended. Right after returning to Delhi, I joined the AI Cell at NHAI, the National Highways Authority of India. So it is kind of a full circle moment as a year later, after a lot of trial and error, this talk is supposed to be a reflection on what we have been able to build, what surprised us, and what FOSS made possible inside a public-sector organization.

Government organizations are often assumed to be slow adopters of new technology, and for good reason, their structure has those constraints and inertia to make them so. At the same time, outside of coding tools, enterprise AI adoption for knowledge work products has been slow, shallow, or stuck at the demo stage.

Our experience at NHAI has complicated both assumptions.

With a small team of designers and engineers, working closely with NHAI insiders, we have been able to build a set of internal AI and productivity tools for the organization.

Marg Sarthi, NHAI’s internal AI assistant, is the flagship example. In production, it has crossed 15,000+ conversations, 50,000+ questions being asked by 1,000+ internal NHAI employees, with 2 out of 3 being repeat users coming back at least once a week.

That gave us a chance to ask why this worked as a daily workflow tool when many internal AI assistants struggle to gain their footing beyond demos. People use it not as a generic chat interface, but for work they already do: finding policy circulars, interpreting clauses, drafting notes and letters, querying project data, working with scanned data heavy PDFs, and navigating approval-heavy processes.

Along with this, across NH-AI, we have built smaller tools as well, from document utilities to workflow-specific assistants. A pattern that we see emerging: each useful tool had builders on one side and an organizational counterpart on the other who pushed for these tools and iterated with us quickly. These institutional co-creators helped translate messy internal needs into product direction: what users would trust, what workflows mattered, and where governance boundaries could not be hand-waved away.

FOSS has mattered tremendously in us being able to make this possible, because it gave this small team agency, often rare in a process led traditional organization. In a closed vendor-led setup, every meaningful change can become a request: wait for procurement, wait for roadmap alignment, wait for customization, wait for integration support. In our case, the ability to run, inspect, adapt, and extend open systems meant that user feedback could turn into working software quickly.

One particular OSS - LibreChat became the base of a tool like Margsarthi and gave us a hackable foundation for the assistant along with MCP giving us a way to connect tools and data without rebuilding the whole chat layer. Forgejo and self-hostable observability tools helped us keep ownership of the development and feedback loop.

This led to us working with proven primitives and being able to ship faster. AI has made this even more powerful. A small team could understand unfamiliar open-source codebases faster, customize them around our workflows, and build tools that would have been too slow to attempt if every change depended on an external vendor cycle.

We do not think that we have a final playbook for government AI, but we have arrived at hints of it as we do have a real production story from inside one public institution: how FOSS and AI helped us move faster, customize deeper, avoid vendor-roadmap bottlenecks, and build tools close enough to daily work that people actually used them.

This talk shares what we learned from that journey, and why the future of AI in government may depend as much on open infrastructure and institutional co-creators as it does on base models.
keyTakeaways: One lesson from this work is that adoption is often a timing problem. In large organizations, the need may be real, but by the time a vendor cycle, procurement loop, or customization request produces something usable, the workflow has shifted or users have already found a workaround.

We want attendees to see how FOSS changes that loop: not just by reducing cost, but by giving institutions the ability to inspect, adapt, host, observe, and replace the systems they depend on. Because the team could build on open, extensible systems and stay close to NHAI stakeholders, feedback could turn into working software quickly enough for users to try it in their daily workflows.

The talk will also cover why internal co-creators matter. NHAI insiders helped translate organizational needs, trust concerns, and governance boundaries into product direction, so the tools were not just technically possible but institutionally usable.

Finally, we want to make the case for internal AI capacity in government. Vendors can be useful, but transformation cannot be fully outsourced. When a small internal team of designers and engineers works with institutional co-creators and owns enough of the stack, it can adapt faster, learn from users directly, and build systems that are accountable to the organization rather than only delivered to it.

dmsksuju3d.description:
Frappe keeps everything about a form on the server. The fields, the validations, the workflow, and the permissions all live in the DocType and change whenever someone edits it. A mobile app that copies that structure into hardcoded screens breaks the day a DocType gets a new field. To fix it you ship a new build to the Play Store, and a field worker on a weak connection may never download it. Add poor or missing network, where the app has to collect data offline and reconcile it later against a server that has also changed, and building mobile on Frappe gets hard fast. This talk is about how we made it tractable, and the code is open source.

We built two pieces that sit on top of Frappe core.

frappe-mobile-control is a Frappe app in Python (AGPL-3.0). It runs on your existing server and decides what the mobile app may do: which DocTypes appear on the phone and in what order, the minimum app version a user must have, whether the app is in maintenance mode, and how login works (password, mobile OTP, or OAuth with PKCE, with token refresh). You change any of this from Frappe Desk and the phone picks it up on the next sync.

frappe-mobile-sdk is a Flutter package in Dart (MIT). Give it a Frappe site and a config file and it builds a working app. It reads the DocType metadata and renders the form for you, with more than twenty field types including links, child tables, and geolocation. It handles the REST calls, the workflow actions, and role permissions, and it stores data in a local SQLite database that syncs both ways.

Four layers, one sync channel. The server stays the source of truth; the SDK renders forms from metadata and works offline; you build only your own UI and logic.

Offline is the focus of the talk. It is easy to describe and full of sharp edges once real users and real networks show up. What we had to solve, and how:

Collect with no network, survive an interrupted sync, and handle a record edited in two places: resumable cursor, conflict guard, dependency-ordered sync, write-ahead logging with serialized writes, a background isolate, and encryption at rest.

A pull that gets killed halfway on a weak connection should not start over. We save the sync position in SQLite so it resumes from where it stopped.

When a phone uploads a record at the same moment the server sends down a newer copy, the two can clash. We added a guard so neither one silently overwrites the other.

Records often depend on each other: a parent and its child rows, or a record and its attachment. We sync them in order and upload attachments first, so you never store a row that points at a file that is not there yet.

SQLite used to crash when several writes arrived together. We turned on write-ahead logging, made writes happen one at a time, and moved sync onto a separate Dart isolate so the screen never freezes while data moves.

When someone adds a field on the server while a form is open on the phone, the app keeps a fingerprint of the form's structure, notices its copy is stale, and refreshes before saving instead of crashing or dropping the field.

The local database is encrypted on the device, because in our work it holds personal data like Aadhaar numbers that should not sit in plain text on a phone in the field.

A field added on the server, with no app rebuild. The old hardcoded app threw NoSuchFieldError; this one picks the field up on the next sync.

We will demo all of this on a real device, not on slides. We build an app from a config file, add a field on the server and watch it appear after a restart with no new build, put the phone in airplane mode and collect a few records, then come back online and watch them sync. We kill the app mid-sync to show it resume, and edit a record on the server while the phone is offline to show how the conflict is handled.

This is not a prototype. The SDK already runs in production apps that field teams use to collect data for large social-sector programmes, on real phones, in places with little or no connectivity. The demo is the same code those teams run.

Both repositories are open. You can install the server app with bench, pull the SDK from pub.dev, point it at your own Frappe site, and build on it or send a patch.
keyTakeaways: How to drive a mobile app's forms, permissions, and versioning from the Frappe server, so a schema change does not need a new app build.
How to render Frappe DocType forms dynamically in Flutter, including links, child tables, and geolocation, without writing the screens by hand.
How an offline sync engine behaves in the field: resuming an interrupted pull, ordering records that depend on each other, and handling a record edited in two places.
Practical ways to keep offline SQLite stable and safe on a field device: write-ahead logging, one-at-a-time writes, a background sync thread, and on-device encryption.
Where to get the code (MIT SDK on pub.dev, AGPL-3.0 server app) and how to build on it or contribute.

5jvkd5u7mk.description: Rapier is the Rust ecosystem’s flagship physics engine: one codebase that ships 2D and 3D, f32 and f64, native and WebAssembly, with optional cross-platform determinism and full state snapshots. This talk uses a live, walkable browser world (built with Runek, a procedural 3D component registry) as the demo, then digs into what Rapier does right as a Rust project: arena-and-handle API design, structure-of-arrays data layout, a clean WASM boundary, and feature-flagged determinism. We’ll compare it honestly against Avian, Jolt, PhysX, and the JS incumbents, and pull out lessons for any Rust crate that targets WASM.

96gh03hfud.description:
Contribute to open source. This is the advice almost everyone in the FOSS community has given or received. Well said. But most newcomers hit a wall, especially the ones who don’t come with a technical background. How do we lower the barrier of entry? Is there a starting point that gently takes someone from being interested to becoming a contributor?

Documentation is one of the most impactful yet underserved areas in open source. It is also one of the most accessible places to begin. The Open Documentation Academy is a free, open programme designed around exactly this idea. It connects people who want to contribute to open source with real documentation tasks on real projects along with mentorship, structured guidance, and a community to work with. This talk introduces the Open Documentation Academy initiative led by technical authors at Canonical and invites new contributors to participate.

If you are looking for an entry point into open source, then this talk is for you.
keyTakeaways: Introduction to Open Documentation Academy
How to join as a contributor
Collaborate with the academy: bring a project in
Ideas for writing better beginner-friendly documentation issues in their own projects

clniq3em1j.description:
Documentation is one of the most important parts of a software project, yet the experience of writing it often feels far behind the experience of writing code. Modern IDEs provide features such as diagnostics, syntax highlighting, code navigation and instant feedback while programming, but documentation authors frequently discover broken links, invalid references and structural issues only after generating the final documentation.

This talk explores how language-server technology can help bridge that gap by bringing IDE-style feedback and navigation to documentation workflows. Through the lens of my Google Summer of Code project with SourceKit-LSP, I will discuss how documentation can be treated as a first-class artifact rather than plain text, enabling richer tooling and a faster feedback loop for writers and maintainers.

I will begin with a brief overview of my journey into open source and how it led me to work on developer tooling through GSoC. From there, the talk will focus on the broader ecosystem of documentation tooling: what documentation compilers are, why documentation workflows often lack the tooling available for source code and how language servers power modern editor experiences.

Using DocC, Apple's documentation compiler for Swift and Objective-C, as a case study, I will explain how language-server concepts such as diagnostics, syntax highlighting and navigation can be applied to documentation files. The talk will also cover the architecture of SourceKit-LSP, the challenges involved in extending language-server functionality to new document types and the design decisions made while implementing support for DocC.

The session will conclude with a live demonstration showing how documentation authors can benefit from IDE features directly while writing documentation, reducing context switching and catching issues before documentation is built.
keyTakeaways: Why documentation should be treated as a part of the development workflow rather than plain text.
How language servers power features such as diagnostics, code navigation, and editor intelligence.
How language-server techniques can be applied beyond programming languages to documentation and other structured content.
What challenges arise when extending language servers to support new document types and workflows.
Practical insights into contributing to large open-source developer tooling projects.

db4ufng84v.description:
I've been working with Bruno, an open source API client, for more than two years and have been closely involved in building and maintaining its documentation from the ground up. While documenting both small and large features, I learned a lot about what works, what doesn't, and how documentation can become a growth driver for an open source project.

In this talk, I'll share real examples, mistakes we made, approaches that failed, and lessons that helped us improve the overall documentation experience. I'll cover topics such as creating an effective starter guide for new users, using analytics not just to measure page views but to understand where users struggle, and using product mockups to explain complex workflows that are difficult to communicate through text alone.

I'll also talk about our experience evaluating documentation platforms such as Nextra, Docusaurus, and MkDocs, and the lessons we learned while improving discoverability, searchability, and documentation structure.

As AI-powered search and agents become a growing source of traffic, documentation also needs to be structured in a way that is easier for machines to understand and retrieve.

Target Audience - This talk is intended for open source maintainers, technical writers, Developer Relations professionals, developer advocates, product engineers, and contributors who are responsible for creating or maintaining documentation for developer-focused products.

Conclusion - Attendees will learn a practical framework for designing documentation that improves onboarding, increases discoverability, reduces support overhead, and drives both open source community growth and product adoption.
keyTakeaways: Why Starter Guides Matters - The starter guide is often the first interaction users have with your product. I'll explain how a well-designed onboarding flow can help users experience value quickly and improve adoption.

How to Use Product Mockups Effectively - People often understand visuals faster than written explanations. I'll discuss when mockups are more effective than text, how we use them in documentation, and the challenges of keeping them updated as the product evolves.

Improving Documentation Search Experience - What users search for is not always how documentation is organized. I'll share practical approaches to structuring titles, navigation, and content around user intent. For example, a user may search for "developer tools" while the documentation refers to the same concept as "debugging tools."

How to Make Documentation AI-Friendly - As more content is consumed through AI tools and agents, documentation needs to provide clear context and structure. I'll share practical techniques for making documentation easier to discover, understand, and retrieve through modern AI-powered experiences.

How Feedback Loop Work - Continuous feedback from different sources is essential for improving documentation. Whether it comes from GitHub issues, community discussions, support requests, or analytics, feedback helps you understand what users are struggling with and where documentation gaps exist.

en28h8l81s.description:
I did engineering, but I'd never really call myself a developer. I was always more drawn to how policy shapes technology than to building the technology itself. For a long time, those two worlds felt separate. Then AI happened, and suddenly the gap between "I wonder if this exists" and "I just built it" collapsed to a weekend.

In 2025, I attended IndiaFOSS for the first time. I'd been to a lot of policy and tech conferences, but this one felt different; there was a genuine energy in the room. People were passionate about what they were building, and more importantly, why. Submitting this proposal for IndiaFOSS 2026 feels like a full-circle moment.

For the last few months, I’ve been trying to understand how India's government actually built its digital infrastructure. I was more interested in the ground-level account of what worked, what didn't, and who made it happen rather than press releases and policy documents. That trail led me to the NIC Informatics newsletter.

The National Informatics Centre has been the invisible backbone of India's digital government for over 50 years — election results, land records, passport systems, Aarogya Setu. For 34 of those years, NIC published a quarterly newsletter called Informatics, documenting what it built and how. 3,865 articles. 1,852 authors. Public servants from every Indian state writing about the systems that now run the country.

The only problem was that all of it was sitting in unsearchable PDFs on a government website. You couldn't Ctrl+F it. You couldn't search across issues. You couldn't find stories and correlations unless you knew exactly where to look. So I decided to build it.

I spent a few weekends with some open source tools and cheap LLM APIs (no serious coding involved) and tried to build an archive that might change that. Here’s a glimpse of a few things I found that surprised me:

This talk is the story of how I stumbled into the project, what I found when I got there, and what I think it means. The code is commoditised. Curiosity is the hard part. A lot of public data in India is technically available, but available and usable are very different things. With the tools we now have, there's no excuse for the gap between the two.
keyTakeaways: Public data and usable data are not the same thing. Availability means nothing without searchability.
With current AI tools, the barrier to building public commons is lower than it's ever been. The entire NIC Archives cost under Rs 500 to build.
India's institutional knowledge is quietly sitting in PDFs. The first step is finding it, the second is making it findable for everyone else.
You don't have to be a developer to use technology for public good. You just have to be curious.

9cl0lf8t0j.description:
Open source has never had more contributors, and yet, more and more projects struggle with adoption, onboarding, and retention. Ever wondered why?

The bottleneck isn't code quality. It's the experience. More specifically the Contributor experience. Bad READMEs, undocumented APIs, broken setup scripts, and hostile first-timer experiences kill more projects every year than any technical limitation ever will.

Developer experience is now the highest-leverage contribution you can make to open source. Yet it remains the most overlooked.

In this talk, we will prove it with evidence. We'll share concrete examples of what broke and what we fixed across API ecosystems and cloud-native infrastructure: onboarding flows that cut time-to-first-PR, documentation architectures that actually scaled, API design decisions that reduced support burden, and contributor ladder structures that turned drive-by visitors into long-term contributors and maintainers. If you care about scaling your open source project, this talk is for you.
keyTakeaways: Is Developer Experience just contributing to documentation?
How most open source projects unintentionally become uninteresting to people before their first move (and how the reason is almost never technical difficulty)?
Why you are loosing contributors? Bad onboarding, broken setup scripts, and outdated docs.
How small DevX fixes like better READMEs, clearer error messages, faster setup, etc. have outsized impact on contributor retention/product success.
How Contributor ladders designed intentionally can turn one-time visitors into long-term maintainers.
A practical DevX audit framework that works on any open source project, regardless of size or ecosystem

6dpd2lbkma.description:
Docs-as-code borrowed a lot from software engineering. Docs live in Git, go through review, run through CI, and ship as versioned sites. Most editors still treat a documentation project as plain text, so the moment you rename a heading, move a page, or split a topic, cross-links and anchors can break with nobody noticing until a reader hits a 404.

I'm a technical writer, and most of my open-source contributions are documentation work, so I keep meeting this problem from the inside. Recently I fixed a few links in the Fluree DB docs that 404'd because mdBook rewrites source .md links to .html but renders a README.md as index.html; a link check then surfaced more broken links across the site. In CocoIndex, I restored links that broke when a release branch was removed, and earlier added a lychee link-checking workflow to its docs CI. The projects and tools differ, but the failure is the same: change the structure, links rot, and CI tells you only after the damage is already public.

This lightning talk treats that as a refactoring problem, not only a writing or publishing one. I'll use Zensical Studio, a newly launched FOSS extension for VS Code, as a worked example of what editor-integrated docs tooling can do: flag broken links as you type, parse Python Markdown the way MkDocs and Zensical read it, and show every incoming link to a heading so one rename updates them all instead of leaving cleanup to CI.
keyTakeaways: Documentation has a refactoring problem that's separate from writing or publishing it. Renaming a heading or moving a page can break links, and most editors won't warn you.
Broken links and shifting anchors erode reader trust. CI catches them, but only after you push.

Editor-integrated tooling can make structural changes safer. I'll use Zensical Studio to show what that looks like in practice: in-editor broken-link diagnostics, Python Markdown awareness for MkDocs and Zensical, and renames that fix incoming links.

76r6ku6p9h.description:
Large open source projects do not only need documentation. They also need memory.

Kubernetes moves through hundreds of issues, pull requests, merges, enhancements, deprecations, release updates, meetings, and discussions. A changelog can tell you what changed, but it often cannot tell a new contributor what deserves attention, why something matters, where to look next, or how a project is moving as a community.

This talk is about Last Week in Kubernetes Development, or LWKD, a weekly newsletter that summarizes Kubernetes development activity: code merges, PRs, deprecations, version updates, release schedules, and community meetings. LWKD is a Kubernetes SIG Contributor Experience project, and its repository contains the Markdown files used to produce the weekly updates, with contributions accepted through pull requests.

I will use my experience as a writer and editor for LWKD to talk about technical writing as a real open source contribution path. The talk will explain how editorial judgment works in a fast-moving FOSS project: deciding what is worth including, summarizing technical changes without flattening nuance, preserving uncertainty, linking claims to sources, making review easy, and helping readers orient themselves inside a large project.

The talk is also prescriptive. I will share a practical contribution path for people who want to enter FOSS through writing: how to pick a recurring publication or documentation surface, study its format, start with one small section, summarize one technical change, cite the source, handle review on prose, and build consistency over time.

The goal is to show that writing in open source is not a fallback for people who do not code. In large projects, writing is infrastructure. It helps communities remember what changed, why it mattered, and how contributors can participate.
keyTakeaways: Why large FOSS projects need community memory, not just documentation, changelogs, and release notes.
What LWKD is, how it helps Kubernetes contributors stay updated, and how a weekly technical newsletter can support contributor experience.
How technical writing becomes a real contribution path in open source, especially for newcomers who are still learning the codebase.
How to summarize fast-moving technical work without losing accuracy, context, or nuance.
How editorial judgment works in FOSS writing: what to include, what to omit, how to cite sources, and how to separate fact from interpretation.
How prose review differs from code review, and why feedback on wording, structure, and framing is part of maintainership.
A practical starting path for new documentation contributors: read existing editions, pick one section, summarize one change, submit a pull request, respond to review, and repeat.
Why writing is not a consolation prize in open source. It is one of the ways communities scale knowledge, trust, and participation.

eqr1r1mp5b.description:
Your documentation now has a second reader, and it reads nothing like the first. Alongside the human skimming for an answer, an LLM or agent is pulling fragments of your docs to answer a question or drive a workflow, and the two readers want opposite things.

A person reads top to bottom, follows a screenshot, and fills gaps from context. An agent pulls one isolated chunk, ignores the layout entirely, cannot see the screenshot, and falls apart when the real meaning was in a diagram or an unstated assumption. The same page that works fine for a human can hand an agent a confidently wrong answer.

This talk shows what actually changes when you write for both. It covers structuring content so a retrieval system returns a correct, self-contained answer, what conventions like llms.txt do, and exposing docs through the Model Context Protocol so an agent queries them at runtime instead of scraping a rendered page. It is also honest about the cost: optimizing for machines can flatten the voice and context that make docs good for humans, and some advice going around right now trades real quality for retrieval scores.

What this talk covers:

How an agent reads your docs differently from a human, shown concretely

Structuring content for self-contained retrieval without dumbing it down

What llms.txt and MCP actually solve, and what they do not

A live look at the same docs page answered well versus badly by an agent

A page-by-page rule for when to optimize for the machine and when to refuse

This is for anyone maintaining docs for an open source project who has noticed AI assistants quoting those docs and wants them to be right.
keyTakeaways: Audit one of your own doc pages for how an agent would actually read it
Restructure a page so that a retrieval system returns a complete, correct chunk
Decide what belongs in llms.txt or an MCP server versus the human-facing page
Tell the difference between machine-readability that helps and advice that just wrecks your docs

7dfgb98p8p.description:
Most people in India learn to code in their second or third language. The syntax is hard enough. Then the documentation, the part that's supposed to help, is in English too. For a learner who thinks in Tamil, that's two walls instead of one.

We decided to take one of those walls down. Our team has been translating Python's official documentation into Tamil, and this isn't a fork or a side-blog. It's the real thing. The translation has been officially recognized by the Python Software Foundation's CPython Core Developers and is now part of Python's official documentation translation effort, listed alongside the other languages Python ships docs in.

This talk is the honest story of how that happened, and how anyone in the room can do it for their own language.

I'll walk through the actual machinery: how Python governs translated documentation under PEP 545, how the docs are structured as Sphinx .po files, how the translation work flows through the coordination process, and the completion bar you have to clear before Python will publish your language officially. None of this is obvious from the outside, and that opacity is exactly why most language communities never start.

Then the harder part, the part no tool solves. There is no settled Tamil word for "iterator," "decorator," or "thread." Every contributor has an opinion. Keeping terminology consistent across thousands of strings, recruiting people who know both Tamil and Python well, and keeping reviewers from burning out turned out to be the real project. The code was the easy bit.

I'll close on why this matters beyond Python. Localization is one of the most underrated forms of FOSS contribution. It needs no deep systems knowledge, it directly widens who gets to participate in open source, and almost every major FOSS project has docs sitting in English waiting for someone to start. By the end, you'll know how to be that someone.

c9kecg3h9i.description:
Every documentation failure has a technical explanation. The heading structure was inconsistent. The error message did not suggest a fix. The getting-started guide assumed the reader already had the environment configured. The warning was buried three paragraphs below the command it was warning about.

But underneath every one of these failures is the same root cause: the writer forgot what it felt like to not know the thing.

This talk is about empathy as a documentation practice, not the soft, abstract kind, but the specific, actionable kind that changes how you write an error message, structure a tutorial, or decide what context to include before a code example. As a technical writer at Red Hat and an open source contributor, I have audited documentation that was technically correct, structurally sound, and completely useless to the person who needed it most because it was written from the inside out rather than the outside in.

We will look at four concrete places where empathy breaks down in documentation: the assumptions we bake in without declaring them, the context we omit because it feels obvious, the error guidance we write for ourselves rather than for someone in a panic at a broken terminal, and the accessibility failures that signal to entire categories of users that this documentation was not written for them. Each failure mode gets a real example, a diagnosis, and a fix.

The talk is structured around a simple provocation: the user who cannot follow your documentation is not failing. Your documentation is failing them. And in open source, where documentation is often the only onboarding a new contributor or user gets, that failure has a direct cost to community health, contributor retention, and the long-term sustainability of the project.

Empathy is not a personality trait. It is a skill, and it can be taught, practised, and built into review processes. This talk shows you how.
keyTakeaways: The four specific places empathy breaks down in technical documentation are assumed knowledge, missing context, poor error guidance, and inaccessible design, with real before and after examples
How to audit your own documentation for empathy failures without needing user research infrastructure, practical techniques any contributor can use today
Why "the user is confused" is rarely the right diagnosis and how reframing documentation failures as empathy failures changes how you fix them
How to build empathy checkpoints into documentation review processes so that individual writers do not have to carry the entire cognitive load alone
A reframe of documentation quality from correctness and completeness to usefulness and welcome, and what that shift means for how FOSS projects prioritise their writing work

0hs9gpkgp4.description:
The PDF file format has stood the test of time as a versatile and highly portable means to producing print-oriented media, reports, documents, and knowledge works, to facilitate information exchange in varied settings. This talk advocates for the proliferation of distributing FOSS project documentation in the PDF file format. I would like to highlight various incentives towards such a paradigm where documentation is browsed offline, while also being balanced and offering a sense into its pitfalls.

While most projects consider offline documentation (via PDF, and other formats such as EPUB) as an afterthought in comparison to web-based documentation, there is a case to be made for it—as a missed opportunity—to reach a wider variety of users. A well-structured PDF is something a documentation website cannot replicate easily – it works without an internet connection, works on all sorts of PDF readers and devices, offers features such as annotations, comments, can go places on compact data storage devices such as flash drives, and lastly, can be printed and handed over to users in the form of manuals and booklets. This matters for remote and low-resource regions with limited internet access – for instance, in countries where metered mobile data costs are high and broadband being evenly distributed is a privilege. Another benefit is accessibility, in that it is easier for a PDF with a semantic heading structure to be more navigable with a screen reader, than a documentation site that may layer custom JavaScript navigation widgets over its content.

The most common form of PDF/offline documentation generation is via typesetting tools such as LaTeX, but the tooling landscape in the world of FOSS has changed considerably, having gone through various advancements – to the point where LaTeX is not the sole choice for a FOSS project wanting to share offline documentation. For instance:

Besides documentation authors, there are also projects for users, i.e., documentation readers. Offline documentation readers, such as Zeal are worth knowing about and pointing to.

However, as can be expected, there are also pitfalls to offline documentation, such as math rendering differences across tools, SVG and figure handling, font embedding, maintaining the accessibility conformance of the generated outputs, how EPUB fares across different reader applications, and maintenance questions of who takes up building documentation for such formats and keeps it going.

Here is a proposed (read: provisional) outline of my talk:
keyTakeaways: A practical survey of FOSS tools for building offline (PDF/EPUB) documentation, with enough specifics to evaluate tradeoffs for your project
A case for offline documentation, including accessibility and connectivity arguments, and how it serves different user needs
Specific failure modes to anticipate in offline builds before they find you in production
When not to build offline documentation

4v0vd3g01j.description:
Building an Android keyboard is fundamentally different from building a traditional Android application. Keyboards operate inside a unique part of the Android ecosystem interacting directly with the Input Method Framework (IMF), communicating across applications, handling sensitive user input, and operating under strict performance and lifecycle constraints.

In this session, I will use lessons from maintaining Scribe-Android, an open-source keyboard project, as a practical case study to explore how Android keyboards (IMEs) actually work. We will examine the architecture behind IME, input flows, lifecycle behavior, and the challenges of building software that integrates deeply with the Android system while interacting seamlessly with other applications.

The talk will also cover real-world engineering challenges encountered while building a production keyboard experience: lifecycle quirks, latency and responsiveness tradeoffs, multilingual input support, debugging behavior across fragmented Android devices, and privacy and security considerations unique to keyboard software.

Rather than serving as a project showcase, this talk uses a real-world open-source IME to explore Android system behavior, architectural decisions, and the engineering tradeoffs required to build responsive, privacy-conscious input experiences.
keyTakeaways: Understand how Android keyboards (IMEs) work and integrate with the Input Method Framework
Learn core IME architecture: IME input flows, and system interaction
Explore engineering tradeoffs around lifecycle behavior, latency, multilingual input, and performance
Understand UI tradeoffs between XML and Compose in the Keyboard Layouts
Learn debugging strategies for OEM quirks, fragmented Android environments, and platform changes (including API 36 breakages)
Understand privacy and security considerations in keyboard software
Gain deeper insight into Android internals through building unconventional system-facing software

41r3mau7ga.description: Android is transitioning from HIDL to Stable AIDL to improve HAL interface stability and long-term maintainability. However, many production devices still depend on legacy HIDL implementations, making upgrades difficult.This talk presents a migration of a HAL from HIDL to Stable AIDL, focusing on real-world challenges. It covers key differences in interface definition, versioning, Binder IPC, and VINTF compatibility. The session walks through a step-by-step migration: rewriting interfaces, updating services, and modifying manifests.Hands-on guide for engineers who must modernize existing HIDL HALs to Stable AIDL in shipping devices.
keyTakeaways: Explain the core architectural differences between HIDL and AIDL in the Android HAL stack.
List the Android version milestones that make AIDL mandatory for new and production devices.
Execute a step-by-step HIDL → AIDL migration for a real hardware interface.
Address SELinux policy changes, VINTF manifest updates, and compatibility matrix versioning required by the migration.
Identify and mitigate common failure, validation.

Many Android phones come with heavy vendor skins and a lot of Google services built in. I wanted something lighter and more private, so I moved from that setup to a custom ROM with less Google dependence.

That shift was not smooth. I ran into soft bricks, a hard brick, SafetyNet and Play Integrity problems, and notifications that did not always behave the way they should. I also tried microG, but in the end I went with a fully vanilla custom ROM setup because that fit my privacy goals better. Along the way, I managed to fix most of the issues I ran into, but a few things never really had a clean or satisfying fix.

For family devices, though, a fully degoogled setup did not make sense. They needed something that was easier to live with, so those phones stayed on a normal GApps-based custom ROM. That ended up being one of the biggest lessons for me: the same setup that feels fine for one person can be too much trouble for someone else.

This talk is about that move, the things that broke along the way, the fixes that worked, the things that stayed broken, and the trade-offs between privacy and daily use.

How to read hardware sensors from a native C++ daemon using standard Linux kernel ABIs
How uinput works and why it is sometimes the right way to talk to Android audio from vendor code
How to write and debug SELinux policy for a vendor service from scratch
The difference between BOARD_VENDOR_SEPOLICY_DIRS and PRODUCT_PRIVATE_SEPOLICY_DIRS and why it matters
How to iterate on a vendor service without reflashing the entire image

beqsttjcbn.description: Have you ever stopped to think about what actually happens inside your smartphone the second you tap an app icon? Instead of booting up from scratch every single time , our phone uses a shortcut to clone a ready to go template which is why our apps launch in the blink of an eye.We build apps every day , many complex ones as well relying on APIs that make UI magically appear but how many of us actually understand the heavy lifting happening underneath? This talk will cover that black box of Android’s operating system for developers who want to look past the surface layer. Did you know that the app doesn’t boot a fresh JVM every time but instead forks from a pre warmed Zygote process to launch instantly. Most importantly, because this entire operating system is open - source , you never have to just guess how things work , we can actually read the blueprints. I’ll show you how to navigate this massive public codebase so you can look up exactly what happens under the hood whenever you get stuck
keyTakeaways: Understand the Zygote forking model and why Android app startup is fast
Know the journey from tapping an icon -> process creation -> first frame on screen
Understand how Compose's compiler plugin + slot table architecture differs from the legacy View system

coqs2rc43i.description:

Explain how AIDL-based HALs fit into the modern Android architecture.
Create and integrate a Rust-based HAL in AOSP.

bb06npb4u0.description:
Launcher3 is one of the most frequently used yet least understood applications in the Android ecosystem. Every interaction on an Android device eventually flows through it, unlocking the device, launching applications, accessing widgets, navigating recent tasks, searching for content, or interacting with personalized experiences such as Google Feed.

Over the last year, while maintaining and customizing Launcher3 across multiple Android releases, I repeatedly dived into parts of the launcher that are rarely documented and even less frequently discussed in public. Many Android developers work on Launcher3, but few get the opportunity to understand why it is structured the way it is. This talk aims to bridge that gap.

Launcher3 is not just an app that opens other apps. It is one of the central part of the Android experience, such as navigation, recents, search, widgets and personalisation. This session will cover its core architecture, workspace, states, and integration with SystemUI. We will also examine how OEMs and custom ROMs extend the same codebase to create different launcher experiences

A major focus of the session will be understanding the architecture behind the Google Feed (-1) screen. Through practical examples and analysis, we will explore how overlay provider plugin communicate with Launcher3, how overlay services are implemented, and what developers can learn when building their own custom launcher experiences.

Along the way, I will also share real-world lessons learned from maintaining Launcher3 customizations, debugging launcher issues across Android releases, and studying the components that make modern Android launchers feel seamless to users.
